echoes.note: Paul's explicit 'for it is written' citation, 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people,' is a near-verbatim quotation of Exod 22:28 (LXX 22:27, 'a ruler of your people you shall not curse'). High Volume (formula + verbatim match) and high Thematic Coherence (Paul submits to the Torah he is accused of violating). Recurrence: the same verse underlies Eccl 10:20. Plausible and historically apt for a Pharisee.

'You whitewashed wall!' draws on Ezekiel's oracle against false prophets who daub a flimsy wall with whitewash that God's storm will tear down — a metaphor for hypocritical leaders whose facade conceals coming judgment. Strong Volume (the rare 'whitewash'/wall image) and Thematic Coherence (Ananias, who orders an unlawful blow while presiding 'to judge by the law,' is exposed as a whitewashed hypocrite under judgment). Satisfaction is high: the taunt gains theological bite when heard against Ezekiel.

Paul's protest, 'Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?', echoes the Torah's demand for righteous, impartial judgment. Moderate Thematic Coherence (legal due process violated); lower Volume since there is no verbal borrowing, only the shared juridical ideal.

The unlawful 'strike on the mouth' inverts Deut's regulation that corporal punishment follow a judicial verdict 'according to his wrongdoing' — here Paul is struck before any verdict. Low Volume; the link rests on the contrast between lawful and lawless beating rather than verbal echo.

'I have lived before God in all good conscience until this day' resonates with the biblical ideal of walking 'before God' blamelessly (Gen 17:1; cf. 1 Kgs 9:4). Faint, idiomatic echo of covenantal integrity rather than a targeted citation; Volume is low.

Paul's opening claim of a clear conscience before the assembly recalls Samuel's farewell protest of blameless conduct before all Israel ('whom have I defrauded?'). Thematic parallel of a leader on trial asserting integrity; low Volume, contested.

Paul stakes his case on 'the hope and resurrection of the dead,' the doctrine that splits Pharisee from Sadducee. Dan 12:2 ('many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life') is the clearest OT bodily-resurrection text and the touchstone of the Pharisaic 'hope.' Strong Thematic Coherence and Recurrence (Paul ties his whole defense to this hope across Acts 23-26). Volume rests on the shared, distinctive doctrine rather than wording.

'Your dead shall live, their bodies shall rise' is a second pillar of OT resurrection hope underlying the Pharisaic confession Paul invokes. Good Thematic Coherence; medium confidence because Daniel 12 is the more direct referent and no wording is quoted.

The vision of dry bones revived contributed to Second Temple resurrection belief and may stand behind the Pharisees' confession of resurrection. Low Volume (no verbal contact); included maximally as a contributing OT stream.
'In my flesh I shall see God' is a classic proof-text for bodily resurrection in the very debate Paul provokes. Faint echo; cited for completeness of the resurrection-hope background.

The night vision in which the Lord stands by Paul and says 'Take courage' (be of good cheer) follows the OT pattern of God commissioning a servant for a daunting journey with the charge to be strong/unafraid, classically Josh 1:6-9 at the threshold of a new mission. Medium Thematic Coherence (divine reassurance + mandate to 'go'); Volume moderate via the 'fear not / be strong' formula.

'Do not be afraid... for I am with you to deliver you' to a prophet sent to hostile authorities closely parallels the Lord's nighttime encouragement to Paul before his testimony to kings and Rome. Good coherence with Paul's prophetic-witness role; medium confidence as a type rather than a quotation.

'That same night the LORD appeared to him and said, Do not fear, for I am with you' (to Isaac) is a tight formal parallel: a night theophany of reassurance. Low Volume but strong formal coherence; contested as a specific source.
'Fear not, for I am with you' — the prototypical divine encouragement formula reflected in the Lord's 'Cheer up, Paul.' Faint, generic echo; low Volume.

The forty-plus conspirators bind themselves 'under a curse' (anathema) to eat and drink nothing until they kill Paul. This rash self-imprecatory food-oath echoes Saul's curse that no one eat until evening/until vengeance is done — an oath that scripture frames as misguided and self-entrapping. Medium Thematic Coherence (a reckless binding oath that cannot be kept); Volume rests on the shared curse-not-to-eat structure.

'They scheme together against me, plotting to take my life' matches the conspiracy 'lying in wait' to kill Paul. The lament-of-the-righteous-pursued pattern (Psalm of David, used in Acts' passion typology for the suffering witness) gives good coherence; medium confidence as thematic echo.
'Let us lie in wait for blood... swift to shed blood' portrays the bloodthirsty ambush the forty plan. Sapiential portrait of murderous conspirators; low Volume, no quotation, but apt coherence.
The wicked who 'lurks in ambush... to seize the poor' mirrors the men who 'lie in wait' for Paul. Generic lament imagery of the ambushing wicked; faint echo, included maximally.

Lysias' elaborate night convoy (two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen) brings Paul 'safely' to Felix, thwarting the sworn plot — a narrative enactment of 'no wisdom or counsel can avail against the LORD; the horse is made ready for battle, but victory belongs to the LORD.' Low Volume, thematic/providential coherence with the divine assurance of v.11.

Paul's deliverance from violent enemies by armed rescue and removal to safety faintly echoes the deliverance-from-foes language of the royal/Davidic psalms ('you delivered me from my enemies... from the violent man'). Generic providence echo; low confidence, contested.
